title: Three Bay Area Hindu Temples Have Been Vandalized in Three Weeks. The DOJ Is Now Involved.
excerpt: Pro-Khalistan graffiti, anti-India slogans, and a theft across Hayward, Newark, and the surrounding area have shaken one of America’s largest Indian diaspora communities.
body:
Three Hindu temples in California’s Bay Area have been targeted by vandals in the span of just a few weeks, in what the Hindu American Foundation is calling a coordinated pattern of hate crimes against the Indian diaspora community. The attacks — involving pro-Khalistan graffiti, anti-India slogans, and a theft — have rattled congregations, drawn condemnation from U.S. lawmakers and the State Department, and prompted India’s External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar to publicly address the incidents.

The most recent attack targeted the Sherawali Temple in Hayward, where pro-Khalistan graffiti was spray-painted on the building’s exterior walls. The incident came two weeks after the Swaminarayan Mandir in nearby Newark was defaced with anti-India and anti-Hindu graffiti in black ink, and one week after a theft was reported at the Shiv Durga Temple in the same area.

## ‘We Won’t Tolerate Them Here’

The Newark Police Department is investigating the Swaminarayan Mandir attack as a potential hate crime. Captain Jonathan Arguello said the department was treating the vandalism as a “targeted act” and reviewing surveillance footage from neighboring residences.

“We’re deeply saddened when these types of acts occur, and we think they’re senseless and they have no room,” Arguello said. “We won’t tolerate them here in Newark. We will investigate as thoroughly as possible with utmost care and sensitivity.”

The U.S. State Department’s Bureau of South and Central Asian Affairs posted a statement on X condemning the attack on the Swaminarayan Mandir and welcoming the Newark Police Department’s efforts to hold those responsible accountable.

Several U.S. lawmakers, including three prominent Indian-American members of Congress, have also spoken out. Representatives Ro Khanna and Michael Waltz, co-chairs of the Congressional Caucus on India, issued a joint statement condemning the incidents and calling on the State Department to coordinate with law enforcement.

## Jaishankar Speaks Out

India’s External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar addressed the vandalism directly in response to a query about the incidents.

“As you know, we are concerned about this. Extremists and separatist forces outside India should not get space,” Jaishankar said. “Our consulate has lodged a complaint with the government and the police there over whatever happened, and I believe the matter is being inquired.”

The Khalistan movement seeks to create an independent Sikh state in India’s Punjab region. A violent Khalistani insurgency was quelled by the Indian government in 1984, and India has designated it a terrorist movement. Overseas, small but vocal pro-Khalistan groups have been linked to periodic vandalism of Hindu temples and Indian diplomatic facilities, particularly in the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

## A Pattern Beyond the Bay Area

The Bay Area incidents are not isolated. The Hindu American Foundation has documented a broader pattern of temple vandalism and anti-Hindu hate crimes across the United States and Canada. Earlier this year, a Lakshmi Narayan temple in Surrey, British Columbia, was vandalized for the third time, with pro-Khalistan graffiti sprayed on its walls and a security camera stolen.

In the United States, online hostility toward Indian Americans surged during the 2024-2025 debates over the H-1B visa program. The broader anti-immigration rhetoric — amplified by both domestic political campaigns and far-right movements — has created an environment where South Asian communities feel increasingly vulnerable.

The HAF has responded by urging temples nationwide to install security cameras and alarm systems. The organization released a safety guide noting that temple graffiti qualifies as a hate crime under federal law and outlining steps for congregations to protect themselves and cooperate with law enforcement.

## What Bay Area Families Are Feeling

For the hundreds of thousands of Indian Americans in the San Francisco Bay Area — one of the largest and most established diaspora communities in the country — the attacks hit close to home in every sense. These are not distant news stories. They are the temples where families gather for Diwali and Navratri, where children attend weekend classes, where elderly parents find community after moving to America.

The Sherawali Temple in Hayward is a family-run shrine operated by immigrants from Fiji, dedicated to the Hindu Goddess Durga. The Swaminarayan Mandir in Newark serves thousands of devotees across the South Bay. These are not political institutions. They are places of worship.

The HAF, the Newark Police, and the Alameda Police Department are all in contact, and the Civil Rights Division of the Department of Justice has been notified. Whether these investigations lead to arrests — and whether the broader pattern of anti-Hindu targeting can be disrupted — remains to be seen.

For now, the temples are installing cameras, the police are reviewing footage, and the congregations are hoping that this is the last time they wake up to graffiti on their walls.
